entities.name: Yaammu Nubwoserre
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Yaammu Nubwoserre reigned as an enigmatic ruler during Egypt's tumultuous Second Intermediate Period, a fragmented era spanning approximately 1650 to 1550 BCE. His reign, traditionally placed around 1560 BCE, falls within a complex political landscape where indigenous Egyptian dynasties coexisted with foreign-origin rulers, particularly the Hyksos of the Fifteenth Dynasty. Nubwoserre's Asiatic name, Ya'ammu, points to his non-Egyptian heritage, a common feature among rulers of the eastern Nile Delta at the time, underscoring the profound demographic and political shifts that characterized this era and challenged the traditional pharaonic state.

The precise placement of Yaammu Nubwoserre within the dynastic sequence remains a subject of scholarly debate. Jürgen von Beckerath, a prominent Egyptologist, traditionally assigned him to the Theban-centric Sixteenth Dynasty, which largely controlled Upper Egypt as a vassal state to the Hyksos. However, more recent research, notably by Kim Ryholt, proposes a different attribution, situating him as the second ruler of the Fourteenth Dynasty. This dynasty, based in Avaris (modern Tell el-Dab'a), consisted primarily of rulers with Semitic names who governed the eastern Nile Delta, often concurrently with the Thirteenth Dynasty in Itjtawy and later Thebes. His reign, regardless of specific dynastic affiliation, reflects the decentralization of power and the strong influence of Levantine populations in Lower Egypt during this period.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Yaammu Nubwoserre represents the fragmented political landscape of the Second Intermediate Period, embodying the presence of non-Egyptian rulers in the Nile Delta before the New Kingdom's reunification. His contested dynastic placement highlights ongoing scholarly efforts to reconstruct a complex era.
